summary: A frequently asked questions document produced by the Internet School Networking group as an introduction to the Internet for teachers, administrators and other school staff. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1941 is a question and answer guide for schools thinking about connecting to the Internet. It covers what a connection costs and what equipment it needs, how to organise it, which Internet services a teacher can use, where to find classroom projects, and how to handle security, objectionable material and rules. It is written for teachers and school administrators rather than for network specialists.

subtitle: A 1996 plain-language Internet primer for teachers and school administrators, written as questions and answers.

tldr.problem: Schools were being asked to connect to the Internet, and the people making that decision, teachers and administrators, had no single place that answered the practical questions: what it costs, what to buy, how to organise it, how to teach with it and how to police it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo is a question and answer document covering the Internet in an educational setting, the cost and shape of a connection, the services and tools available, where classroom projects are advertised, and security, ethics and rules.
tldr.outcome: It is FYI 22, and it replaced the earlier FYI 22 document, RFC 1578, with the FYI number held constant across updates. The prices, services and contacts it lists are from 1996.

today: RFC 1941 is an Informational memo published in May 1996, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is FYI 22 and replaces the earlier FYI 22 document, RFC 1578, with the FYI number held constant across updates. The prices, services and contacts it lists are from 1996.

sections.title: Who the Document Is For
sections.content:
This FYI document was produced by the Internet School Networking group of the User Services Area of the IETF as an introduction to the Internet for faculty, administration and other school personnel in primary and secondary schools. The intended audience is educators who are recently connected to the Internet, who are accessing it by some means other than a direct connection, or who are just beginning to consider Internet access as a resource for their schools.

While the IETF and the Internet School Networking group are international, the authors are experienced only in bringing the Internet to schools in the United States, and the document is limited in focus to internetworking there. They note that culture and the national economy affect how one views the issues around school networking, and that while the document has a United States flavour, they feel the focus will not prevent it from being useful in other countries.

The document is FYI 22. It updates the earlier FYI 22 document, RFC 1578, and renders that document obsolete; the FYI number stays the same if future updates are produced, while the RFC number changes again. For questions of a more general nature the authors recommend FYI 4, "Answers to Commonly Asked 'New Internet User' Questions", and they remind the reader that the Internet is a changing environment, so something listed may be unavailable or may have changed.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a primer for teachers and school administrators who are about to connect a school to the Internet for the first time. It answers questions about cost, equipment, curriculum, security and the rules to set, and it is written for people who are not networking specialists.

sections.title: The Internet in an Educational Setting
sections.content:
The Internet is described as a large and rapidly growing worldwide network of smaller computer networks, all linked by a common protocol, that enables computers of different types to exchange information. The networks are owned by countless commercial, research, government and education organisations and individuals. The memo notes that there is no official governing body, and that the Internet Society serves as the international organisation for Internet cooperation and coordination.

The benefits for a classroom are set out in the answers in this section. The Internet expands the classroom by delivering information, data, images and even computer software from places otherwise impossible to reach, almost instantly, and it brings into the classroom experts in every content area, colleagues and friends in other parts of the world. It shifts the focus away from a teacher-as-expert model and toward one of shared responsibility for learning, and because class, race, ability and disability are removed as factors in communication while using the Internet, it is a natural tool for addressing the needs of all students.

The memo is careful about what the Internet does not replace. Just as textbooks, periodicals, videos, guest speakers and field trips are often used to support a curriculum, the Internet can be used as a tool for teaching and learning, and it need not be the sole instructional method in a classroom. Teachers remain responsible for making informed decisions about the best way to use it. On books, the memo notes that much material published on the Internet lacks the authority of an established publishing house and may need a more critical look, but that assessing information critically is one of the hallmarks of a good education whatever the source. Integrating the Internet into the curriculum means using it to teach content and to reach goals that have already been established, not treating it as an end in itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo argues that the Internet adds reach and freshness to a classroom and lets teachers and students talk to people outside it. It also says plainly that it does not replace the teacher or the textbook, and that it has to serve a lesson already planned rather than become the lesson.

sections.title: Getting the Internet into the School
sections.content:
The cost of a connection varies greatly with the location of the site and the kind of connection that suits the need, and the memo groups users into four kinds: basic individual users, advanced individual users, school networks and school district networks. A basic user wanting a few hours a week is best served by a nationwide online service such as America Online, CompuServe or Prodigy, which gives a simple setup with graphical access screens, using a standard PC or Macintosh and a 14.4 kilobits per second modem. A basic user wanting many hours a day should consider a shell account from a local Internet Service Provider, which gives access to a Unix computer and all the standard services at a cheaper rate, though without a graphical interface. An advanced user, who wants graphical interfaces or wants to offer services to others, should get a SLIP or PPP account.

A school with more than a few individual users needs a network with a high-speed dedicated line, usually a leased line. The memo notes that the connection from the school's LANs needs a CSU/DSU for a digital leased line, or a modem for an analog one, plus a router, and that this is a substantially more difficult setup to manage. A district with several locations should get bids from several providers. The memo also warns about costs that are easy to overlook: technical support and training, equipment maintenance, and on-site expertise. Its general rule for budgeting is that for every dollar spent on hardware and software, plan to spend three dollars to support the technology and those using it.

On organisation, the memo says structures vary widely: in many schools the librarians or media specialists guide the network and its policies, elsewhere an interested teacher drives the project, and the administration has to be behind the plan either way. It recommends making access possible for as many computers as possible, ideally throughout the school on one or more LANs served by a single dedicated connection of 56 Kbs or higher, and notes that where access can be given for only a few computers, at least one of them should be in the library where all students can reach it.
sections.plainLanguage: A school can start small and grow. One computer with a modem is enough to try, a school network on a dedicated line serves everyone at once, and a district needs several providers bidding against each other. The rule of thumb the memo offers is that supporting the equipment and the people using it costs about three times what the equipment itself costs.

sections.title: Using the Internet Services
sections.content:
The memo answers more questions about the World Wide Web than about other services, for three reasons: the Web was the Internet tool coming into most prominence at the time of writing, many of the other services are included seamlessly within it, and getting around with it is easy for people who are not interested in computers. It also warns that finding what you want is not always simple, comparing the Internet to a vast library without a comprehensive card catalog.

The World Wide Web was initiated by CERN in Geneva and is driven by the World Wide Web Consortium. Users navigate by selecting highlighted text that leads to another document or location, called a pointer, a link or an anchor, which makes the exploration of documents three-dimensional rather than flat, and documents can hold text, sound, graphics and moving images. A browser is the client that retrieves and reads documents from Web servers, and every document has a unique address, a URL, a uniform resource locator, which users can type in or which is embedded in the text of another document as a link. Documents on the Web are written in hypertext markup language, HTML, a simple language for formatting text, inserting images and sound, and creating links.

The other services get a paragraph each. Email is probably the most basic tool and is used either between two people or through groups called mail lists. Network news, also called Usenet News, is read with a news reader instead of arriving in a mailbox. FTP transfers files between computers, and anonymous FTP reaches the many public archives. Telnet logs into a computer elsewhere and uses the services there. Gopher browses for information using menus. Searching and indexing tools include Archie for FTP sites, Veronica for Gopherspace, WAIS for indexed databases, and Yahoo, Lycos and WebCrawler for the Web. Videoconferencing over IP was beginning, using MBONE or CU-SeeMe.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo spends most of its space on the World Wide Web, because that was the tool schools were adopting, and because it can reach most other Internet services as well. The rest, such as email, file transfer, telnet, Gopher and newsgroups, are described in a paragraph each so a teacher can recognise what a student or colleague is talking about.

sections.title: Classroom Resources and Collaboration
sections.content:
Once teachers can use the search tools, the memo points them at resources aimed specifically at primary and secondary schools. Among the information servers it lists Global SchoolNet, whose site offers help setting up projects and a registry of projects in which schools can participate, EdWeb, the server of the Consortium for School Networking, NASA's Spacelink and Quest servers with lesson plans, curriculum units and interactive projects, the Empire Internet Schoolhouse hosted by the New York State Education and Research Network, the list of K-12 schools on the Internet maintained on the SENDIT network, the National School Network Testbed project, and the Web pages of the Internet School Networking group itself.

Projects are also advertised on electronic mail lists such as Ednet and Kidsphere, in the K12 hierarchy of Usenet News, and at conferences such as the National Education Computing Conference, Tel-Ed and the Internet Society conference. Many Web sites also list favourite bookmarks for educators. The memo ends this section by pointing the other way: a school can add its own contributions, by sharing knowledge on the mail lists and news groups and by maintaining Web pages to publish student projects and information about the school.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists the places where school projects are advertised: servers run by school networks and by NASA, mail lists, newsgroups and conferences. It also points the other way, noting that a school can publish its own projects rather than only consuming other people's.

sections.title: Security, Ethics and Rules
sections.content:
The memo treats security and ethics together, starting with the question of objectionable material. It notes that sensational media accounts tend to downplay the educational uses of the Internet in favour of the more controversial material available, and that concerned educators should learn about the issue and formulate a strategy before problems arise. It points out that students do not accidentally bump into objectionable material in the course of most educational explorations, and that most find such material only because they are looking for it.

Several responses are described. The most important and effective action is to develop clear policies with rules and consequences, called Acceptable Use Policies, which work best when they line up with the rules governing other behaviour at school. Commercial software can block access to controversial sites, look for specific text in mail, or do both. A proxy server puts all the school's computers behind one machine with full Internet access, and can be configured to mask away objectionable sites; adding a caching server keeps copies of Web pages locally. Filtering store-and-forward mail and news before it is forwarded is another method, as is controlling when students may connect and requiring supervision. The memo is honest that none of the technical solutions had proved wholly successful at the time of writing, and that they may need to be combined with clear policies and with teaching the ethics of Internet access as a matter of course.

On computer security it draws a distinction: a hacker is someone excellent at understanding and manipulating computer systems, and a cracker is someone who maliciously and illegally enters or attempts to enter someone else's system. Not only school policy but also state and national laws may apply, the Site Security Handbook is suggested as a starting point for setting up a security policy, and an intrusion from outside the school should be reported to the CERT Coordination Center. On viruses, it gives two precautions: install virus protection software on all the computers, and use only trusted sources for anything downloaded. For rules, the access provider should acquaint the school with its own Acceptable Use Policy, and the school should establish a school-wide policy in addition, which is usually more restrictive and specific. Beyond those there are no overreaching rules, but there are community standards and conventions to observe.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo's advice is that policy and teaching do more than filtering software. Write down what is allowed and what happens if the rules are broken, keep the computers protected with virus software, download only from sources you trust, and treat the ethics of using the Internet as part of the curriculum. It also says plainly that none of the technical filters had proved wholly successful at the time of writing.

viz.caption: WAYS THE MEMO SUGGESTS FOR HANDLING OBJECTIONABLE MATERIAL

items.title: Acceptable Use Policy
items.text: Rules and consequences set by the school; the action the memo calls most important and effective.

items.title: Filtering software
items.text: Commercial products that block sites, search mail for text, or do both.

items.title: Proxy server
items.text: One machine with Internet access that all school computers go through, able to mask away sites.

items.title: Caching server
items.text: Keeps copies of Web pages locally after fetching them, so a busy site is easier to reach.

items.title: Store-and-forward filtering
items.text: Inspecting queued mail and news before it is forwarded onward.

items.title: Supervised access
items.text: Controlling when students may connect, and allowing it only under supervision.
